      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Diabetes Type 2</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Non-Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus</content>

      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Type 2 Diabetes</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Type 2 diabetes</span> is a disease in which your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose is your main source of energy. It comes from the foods you eat. A hormone called insulin helps the glucose get into your cells to give them energy. If you have diabetes, your body doesn't make enough insulin or doesn't use insulin well. The glucose then stays in your blood and not enough goes into your cells.</p><p>Over time, having too much glucose in your blood can cause health problems. But you can take steps to manage your diabetes and try to prevent these health problems.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Type 2 diabetes</span> may be caused by a combination of factors:</p><ul><li>Being overweight or having obesity</li><li>Not being physically active</li><li>Genetics and family history</li></ul><p><span class="qt0">Type 2 diabetes</span> usually starts with insulin resistance. This is a condition in which your cells don't respond normally to insulin. As a result, your body needs more insulin to help the glucose enter your cells. At first, your body makes more insulin to try to get cells to respond. But over time, your body can't make enough insulin, and your blood glucose levels rise.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>?<p>You are at higher risk of developing <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> if you:</p><ul><li>Are over age 45. Children, teenagers, and younger adults can get <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>, but it is more common in middle-aged and older people.</li><li>Have prediabetes, which means that your blood glucose is high for you but not high enough to be called diabetes</li><li>Had diabetes in pregnancy or gave birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more.</li><li>Have a family history of diabetes</li><li>Are overweight or have obesity</li><li>Are Black or African American, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Asian American, or Pacific Islander</li><li>Are not physically active</li><li>Have other conditions such as high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), or depression</li><li>Have low HDL (good) cholesterol and high triglycerides</li><li>Have acanthosis nigricans - dark, thick, and velvety skin around your neck or armpits</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>?<p>Many people with <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> have no symptoms at all. If you do have them, the symptoms develop slowly over several years. They might be so mild that you do not notice them. The symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Increased thirst and urination</li><li>Increased hunger</li><li>Feeling tired</li><li>Blurred vision</li><li>Numbness or tingling in the feet or hands</li><li>Sores that do not heal</li><li>Unexplained weight loss</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> diagnosed?<p>Your provider will use blood tests to diagnose <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>. The blood tests include:</p><ul><li>A1C test, which measures your average blood glucose level over the past 3 months.</li><li>Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) test, which measures your current blood glucose level. You need to fast (not eat or drink anything except water) for at least 8 hours before the test.</li><li>Random plasma glucose (RPG) test, which measures your current blood glucose level. This test is used when you have diabetes symptoms and the provider does not want to wait for you to fast before having the test.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>?<p>Treatment for <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> involves managing your blood glucose levels. Many people are able to do this by living a healthy lifestyle. Some people may also need to take medicine:</p><ul><li>A healthy lifestyle includes following a healthy eating plan and getting regular physical activity. You need to learn how to balance what you eat and drink with physical activity and diabetes medicine, if you take any.</li><li>Medicines for diabetes include oral medicines, insulin, and other injectable medicines. Over time, some people will need to take more than one type of medicine to control their diabetes.</li><li>You will need to check your blood glucose regularly. Your provider will tell you how often you need to do it.</li><li>It's also important to keep your blood pressure and cholesterol levels close to the targets your provider sets for you. Make sure to get your screening tests regularly.</li></ul>Can <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> be prevented?<p>You can take steps to help prevent or delay <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> by losing weight if you are overweight, eating fewer calories, and being more physically active. If you have a condition which raises your risk for <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>, managing that condition may lower your risk of getting <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title">Diabetes Type 1</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Insulin-Dependent Diabetes Mellitus</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Juvenile Diabetes</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Type 1 Diabetes</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Insulin-dependent diabetes</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Type I diabetes</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is type 1 diabetes?<p>Diabetes means your blood glucose, also called blood sugar, is too high. With type 1 diabetes, your body makes little or no insulin. Insulin is a hormone from your pancreas that helps glucose move from your body into your cells, where it is used for energy. Your body can make glucose, but it also comes from the food you eat. Without insulin, too much glucose stays in your blood. </p><p>Over time, high blood glucose can lead to serious problems with your heart, eyes, kidneys, nerves, gums, and teeth.  </p><p>If your blood glucose gets very high, you can develop diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). It happens when your body doesn't have enough insulin to allow glucose into your cells. Instead, your liver breaks down fat for energy, which produces ketones. When ketones build up too quickly, they can reach dangerous levels. DKA is a life-threatening emergency. </p>What causes type 1 diabetes?<p>Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease. Your immune system mistakenly attacks the cells in your pancreas that make insulin. Researchers don't yet know exactly why this happens. Genes and environmental factors may play a role in triggering the disease. </p>Who is more likely to develop type 1 diabetes?<p>Type 1 diabetes often begins in children and young adults, but it can appear at any age. Having a parent or sibling with type 1 diabetes may increase your chance of developing it. </p>What are the symptoms of type 1 diabetes?<p>Symptoms often start quickly, especially in children. In adults, they may develop more slowly. Symptoms may include: </p><ul><li>Feeling very thirsty </li><li>Feeling very hungry </li><li>Urinating (peeing) more often, including at night </li><li>Having fatigue</li><li>Having blurry vision </li><li>Losing feeling in your feet, or having tingling in your feet or hands </li><li>Having sores that don't heal  </li><li>Losing weight without trying </li></ul>How is type 1 diabetes diagnosed?<p>Blood tests that measure your blood glucose level can show whether it is higher than normal for you. </p>What are the treatments for type 1 diabetes?<p>Type 1 diabetes is a chronic (long-term) condition. You will need daily insulin, either through injections or an insulin pump. Some people also take another diabetes medicine that works with insulin. </p><p>Ask your health care provider about the best way to check your blood glucose level and how often you should check it. </p>Can type 1 diabetes be prevented?<p>Type 1 diabetes can't be prevented. But you may be able to prevent or delay health problems related to diabetes by: </p><ul><li>Managing your blood glucose level with finger prick tests or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) </li><li>Making healthy food choices</li><li>Getting regular exercise</li></ul><p>A blood test called the A1C can show how well you are managing your diabetes over time. </p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title">Diabetes in Children and Teens</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Children and Diabetes</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Teens and Diabetes</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Until recently, the common type of diabetes in children and teens was type 1. It was called juvenile diabetes. With Type 1 diabetes, the pancreas does not make insulin. Insulin is a hormone that helps glucose,or sugar, get into your cells to give them energy. Without insulin, too much sugar stays in the blood.</p><p>Now younger people are also getting <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes.  Type 2 diabetes</span> used to be called adult-onset diabetes. But now it is becoming more common in children and teens, due to more obesity. With <span class="qt0">Type 2 diabetes</span>, the body does not make or use insulin well.</p><p>Children have a higher risk of <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> if they  are overweight or have obesity, have a family history of diabetes, or are not active. Children who are African American, Hispanic, Native American/Alaska Native, Asian American, or Pacific Islander also have a higher risk. To lower the risk of <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> in children:</p><ul><li>Have them maintain a healthy weight</li><li>Be sure they are physically active</li><li>Have them eat smaller portions of healthy foods</li><li>Limit time with the TV, computer, and video</li></ul><p>Children and teens with type 1 diabetes may need to take insulin. <span class="qt0">Type 2 diabetes</span> may be  controlled with diet and exercise. If not, patients will need to take oral diabetes medicines or insulin. A blood test called the A1C can check on how you are managing your diabetes.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/howtopreventdiabetes.html">
      <content name="title">How to Prevent Diabetes</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Diabetes Prevention</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is diabetes?<p>Diabetes, also called diabetes mellitus, is a disease that causes your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels to be too high. There are three types of diabetes: type 1 diabetes, gestational <span class="qt0">diabetes, and type 2 diabetes. Type 2 diabetes</span> is the most common type and may be prevented, delayed, or managed by making lifestyle changes.</p>What is <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>?<p>If you have <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>, your body doesn't make enough insulin or doesn't use it well. This is called insulin resistance. Insulin is a hormone that helps glucose get into your cells. Glucose is your cells' main source of energy and comes from the foods you eat. If your body is resistant to insulin, then insulin can't get enough glucose into your cells. This then leads to glucose staying in your blood, leading to high blood glucose levels.</p><p>Over time, having too much glucose in your blood can cause health problems. If you are at risk for <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>, you might be able to prevent or delay developing it.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>?<p>Many people are at risk for <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>. Your chances of getting it depend on a combination of risk factors such as your genes and lifestyle. The risk factors include:</p><ul><li>Having prediabetes, which means you have blood glucose levels that are high for you, but not high enough to be called diabetes</li><li>Being overweight or having obesity</li><li>Being age 35 or older</li><li>A family history of diabetes</li><li>Being African American, Alaska Native, American Indian, Asian American, Hispanic/Latino, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander</li><li>Having high blood pressure</li><li>Having a low level of HDL (good) cholesterol or a high level of triglycerides</li><li>A history of diabetes in pregnancy</li><li>Having given birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more</li><li>An inactive lifestyle</li><li>A history of heart disease or stroke</li><li>Having depression</li><li>Having polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)</li><li>Having acanthosis nigricans, a skin condition in which your skin becomes dark and thick, especially around your neck or armpits</li><li>Smoking</li></ul>How can I prevent or delay getting <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>?<p>Most of the things that you need to do to prevent or delay getting <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> involve having a healthier lifestyle. Lifestyle changes include:</p><ul><li>Lose weight.Weight control is an important part of diabetes prevention. You may be able to prevent or delay diabetes by losing 5 to 7% of your current weight. For example, if you weigh 200 pounds, your goal would be to lose between 10 to 14 pounds. And once you lose the weight, it is important that you don't gain it back.</li><li>Follow a healthy eating plan. It is important to reduce the amount of calories you eat and drink each day, so you can lose weight and keep it off. To do that, your diet should include smaller portions and less fat and sugar. You should also eat a variety of foods from each food group, including plenty of whole grains, fruits, and vegetables. It's also a good idea to limit red meat and avoid processed meats.</li><li>Get regular exercise. Being physically active has many health benefits, including helping you to lose weight and lower your blood glucose levels. These both lower your risk of <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>. Try to get at least 30 minutes of physical activity on most days of the week. The amount of exercise you need depends on your age and health. Even small amounts of exercise can be helpful. If you have not been active, talk with your health care provider to figure out which types of exercise are best for you. You can start slowly and work up to your goal.</li><li>Don't smoke. Smoking can contribute to insulin resistance, which can lead to <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>. If you already smoke, try to quit.</li><li>Talk to your provider to see whether there is anything else you can do to delay or to prevent <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>. If you are at high risk, your provider may suggest that you take one of a few types of diabetes medicines.</li></ul><p>If you make these changes, you will get other health benefits as well. You may lower your risk of other diseases, and you will probably feel better and have more energy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title">Diabetes</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Diabetes Mellitus</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sugar Diabetes</content>
      <content name="altTitle">DM</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is diabetes?<p>Diabetes, also known as diabetes mellitus, is a disease in which your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose is your body's main source of energy. Your body can make glucose, but it also comes from the food you eat. Insulin is a hormone made by your pancreas. Insulin helps move glucose from your bloodstream into your cells, where it can be used for energy.</p><p>If you have diabetes, your body can't make insulin, can't use insulin as well as it should, or both. Too much glucose stays in your blood and doesn't reach your cells. This can cause glucose levels to get too high. Over time, high blood glucose levels can lead to serious health conditions. But you can take steps to manage your diabetes and try to prevent these health problems.</p>What are the types of diabetes?<p>There are different types of diabetes:</p><ul><li>Type 1 diabetes. If you have type 1 diabetes, your body makes little or no insulin. It happens when your immune system attacks and destroys the cells that produce insulin. </li><li><span class="qt0">Type 2 diabetes</span>. This is the most common form of diabetes. If you have <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>, your body may still be able to make insulin, but your cells don't respond well to insulin. They can't easily take up enough glucose from your blood.</li><li>Gestational diabetes. This is a form of diabetes that develops during pregnancy. It happens when your body can't make the extra insulin it needs during pregnancy.</li></ul>What causes diabetes?<p>The different types of diabetes have different causes:</p><ul><li>Researchers think type 1 diabetes is caused by genes and factors in the environment that might trigger the disease.</li><li><span class="qt0">Type 2 diabetes</span> is caused by several factors, including lifestyle factors and genes. The lifestyle factors include not being physically active and being overweight or having obesity.</li><li>Researchers think gestational diabetes is caused by the hormonal changes of pregnancy along with genetic and lifestyle factors.</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop diabetes?<p>The different types of diabetes have different risk factors:</p><ul><li>You can develop type 1 diabetes at any age, but it most often starts in childhood. Having a parent or sibling with type 1 diabetes may increase your chance of developing it.</li><li>You are at higher risk of developing <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> if you:</li><ul><li>Are overweight or have obesity.</li><li>Are over age 35. Children, teenagers, and younger adults can get diabetes, but it is more common in middle-aged and older adults.</li><li>Have a family history of diabetes.</li><li>Have prediabetes. This means that your blood glucose is higher than normal, but it's not high enough to be called diabetes.</li><li>Had gestational diabetes.</li><li>Have given birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more.</li><li>Are African American, American Indian, Asian American, Hispanic/Latino, or Pacific Islander.</li><li>Are not physically active.</li><li>Have certain other health conditions, such as high blood pressure or polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).</li></ul><li>You are at higher risk of developing gestational diabetes if you:</li><ul><li>Are overweight or have obesity.</li><li>Have a family history of diabetes.</li><li>Had gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy.</li><li>Have given birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more.</li><li>Have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).</li><li>Are African American, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander.</li></ul></ul>What are the symptoms of diabetes?<p>The symptoms of diabetes may include:</p><ul><li>Feeling very thirsty</li><li>Feeling very hungry</li><li>Urinating (peeing) more often, including at night</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Blurry vision</li><li>Numbness or tingling in the feet or hands</li><li>Sores that do not heal</li><li>Losing weight without trying</li></ul><p>But it's important to know that your symptoms may vary, depending on which type you have:</p><ul><li>The symptoms of type 1 diabetes usually come on quickly and can be severe.</li><li>With <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>, the symptoms often develop slowly, over several years. The symptoms can be so mild that you might not even notice them.</li><li>Gestational diabetes often has no symptoms. If you do have symptoms, they may be mild. If you are pregnant, you will usually be screened for this condition between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. </li></ul>How is diabetes diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have diabetes, your health care provider will use one or more glucose blood tests. There are several types, including the A1C test.</p>What are the treatments for diabetes?<p>Treatment for diabetes involves managing your blood glucose levels:</p><ul><li>If you have type 1 diabetes, you will need to take daily doses of insulin, either by injection or through a special pump. Some people also need to take another type of diabetes medicine that works with insulin.</li><li>If you have <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span>, you may be able to manage or even reverse it by making lifestyle changes. These include eating a healthy diet, staying at healthy weight, and getting regular physical activity. Some people also need to take diabetes medicines to manage their diabetes.</li><li>If you have gestational diabetes, you may be able to lower your glucose levels by eating a healthy diet and getting regular exercise. But be sure to talk to your provider about your treatment options. Gestational diabetes usually goes away after you give birth. But you will have a higher risk of developing <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> later.</li></ul><p>Checking your blood glucose levels is also an important part of managing your diabetes. Ask your provider about the best way to check your blood glucose level and how often you should check it.</p>Can diabetes be prevented?<p>Type 1 diabetes can't be prevented.</p><p>You may be able to delay or prevent <span class="qt0">type 2 diabetes</span> through the same lifestyle changes that are used to manage diabetes (eating a healthy diet, staying at a healthy weight, and getting regular physical activity). These lifestyle changes may also help prevent gestational diabetes.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>
